security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown links, inline code, jq parsing, standard redirection, and multilingual text. I confirmed the cross-skill prerequisite that leaves the audited package boundary and the Claude auto-reply example as meaningful risks. No prompt-injection instructions were found in the skill files themselves.

remediation.issue: Cross-skill prerequisite uses a parent-directory reference.
remediation.suggestion: Package the shared authentication and safety guidance inside this skill, or declare an audited marketplace dependency.

remediation.issue: The auto-reply example lets untrusted chat content drive bot output.
remediation.suggestion: Add human approval, allowlists, rate limits, and prompt-injection filtering before posting AI-generated replies.

remediation.issue: The document logging example appends message content without sanitization guidance.
remediation.suggestion: Escape untrusted message content and define retention, privacy, and document access controls.

finding_verdicts.reason: The command substitution only pipes a quoted event line into jq to extract a content field. It does not execute user-controlled shell syntax.
The command substitution parses a message_id from quoted NDJSON with jq. This is data extraction, not command execution from untrusted input.

The example runs the Claude CLI using content received from Lark messages, then adjacent lines post the result as a bot reply. Shell quoting reduces command-injection risk, but untrusted message content can drive autonomous AI behavior.
The jq command receives the generated answer through --arg and builds a request body. It does not evaluate the answer as shell code.
The command substitution extracts a content field from quoted input with jq. No shell execution path is created from the event content.
The prerequisite directs the agent to read ../../lark-shared/SKILL.md outside the audited skill directory. That can import unscanned instructions across the package boundary.
This is a reference-list Markdown link to another Lark skill. It is not a runtime file access request or user-controlled path operation.
This is a documentation link to a related Lark document skill. It does not instruct file reads during execution or use external input as a path.
This appears in a References section as a Markdown link. Unlike the prerequisite, it does not actively direct the agent to load external instructions.
The /dev/null redirection prevents the Claude CLI from reading stdin and suppresses stderr. It is standard shell plumbing, not sensitive file access.
The line assigns a message_id parsed from event JSON. It does not enumerate host, network, process, or account information.
The backticks are Markdown formatting around a link target. There is no Ruby code or shell backtick execution in this file.
The backticks format an example command pattern in documentation. The line does not execute the command or interpolate user input.
The backticks are Markdown syntax for a shortcut link in a table. They are not executable code.
The main skill instructs the agent to read ../lark-shared/SKILL.md before use. This crosses the audited package boundary and can pull in instructions not covered by this report.
The high-entropy signal comes from a long Chinese description mixed with English product terms. No encoded payload or encrypted blob is present on the cited line.
SKILL.md is a short Markdown file with YAML front matter and multilingual text. There is no binary content or obfuscated payload.

semantic_findings.title: Autonomous Bot Reply From Untrusted Messages

content.user_title: Subscribe to Lark Events in Real Time
content.value_statement: Teams need a reliable way to observe Lark messages and workspace changes as they happen. This skill guides real-time event subscription with compact output, filters, routing, and file logging.
actual_capabilities: Explains how to subscribe to Lark event streams with lark-cli event +subscribe.
Shows filtering by event type and client-side regular expressions.
Documents compact, raw NDJSON, and pretty JSON output modes.
Describes routing events to stdout, output directories, or regex-selected directories.
Lists common IM, contact, calendar, approval, task, drive, and application events.
Provides pipeline examples for bot replies and document logging.
limitations: Lark Open Platform events and permissions must be configured before events are received.
The subscription uses bot identity with App ID and App Secret.
The CLI cannot dynamically subscribe to events that are not enabled in the console.
Force mode can split delivery across concurrent connections and should be avoided.

use_cases.title: Monitor Workspace Events
use_cases.description: Stream messages, contact changes, calendar changes, and task updates into operational monitoring workflows.

use_cases.title: Build Bot Event Pipelines
use_cases.description: Receive compact message events and route them into reviewed bot response workflows.

use_cases.title: Archive Event Activity
use_cases.description: Write selected events to local files or documents for audit trails and later analysis.

prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for one event stream.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the lark-event skill to show me how to subscribe to Lark message events with compact output.

prompt_templates.title: Filter Event Types
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate setup for focused event intake.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me choose Lark event types and filters for messages, calendar changes, and contact updates.

prompt_templates.title: Route And Store Events
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a Lark event routing setup that separates IM events from contact events and stores them in different folders.

prompt_templates.title: Design Safe Automation
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a reviewed Lark bot automation plan that uses incoming events but requires approval before sending replies or updating documents.

output_examples.input: Need to monitor only incoming Lark messages.
output_examples.output: The assistant recommends the message receive event, compact output, quiet mode, and the required bot permission.

output_examples.input: Need to separate contact and calendar changes.
output_examples.output: The assistant proposes client-side filters, route patterns, and separate storage locations for each event group.

output_examples.input: Need to connect messages to an AI reply workflow.
output_examples.output: The assistant outlines an approval-first workflow with prompt safety checks, rate limits, and reviewed bot replies.

best_practices: Enable only the Lark event types and scopes required for the workflow.
Use compact and quiet output for agent pipelines to reduce noisy fields.
Run one subscriber per app unless split delivery is intentional and handled.
anti_patterns: Do not use force mode to start duplicate listeners without a delivery plan.
Do not send AI-generated replies automatically from untrusted message content.
Do not write event archives to shared folders without retention and access controls.

faq.question: What does this skill help me do?
faq.answer: It helps you subscribe to Lark event streams and process them as compact event output.

faq.question: Does it require user login?
faq.answer: No. The documented subscription uses bot identity with App ID and App Secret.

faq.question: Can it receive any Lark event automatically?
faq.answer: No. Events and permissions must first be enabled in the Lark Open Platform console.

faq.question: Can I route events into files?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill documents output directories and regex-based routing for selected events.

faq.question: Is compact output supported?
faq.answer: Yes. Compact output flattens common event fields for easier agent and script processing.

faq.question: Should I let it reply to messages automatically?
faq.answer: Use review, allowlists, and policy checks before any bot sends AI-generated replies.
